analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil companies and large corporations to fund toxic-waste site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst toxic-waste sites. Its dedicated funding taxes expired in the mid-1990s, shifting cleanup costs onto ordinary taxpayers. This bill would reinstate a per-barrel fee on crude oil at a higher, inflation-adjusted rate through 2023 and add a small 0.12% surtax on corporate income above $3.13 million through 2024, with the money flowing back into the Superfund trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near contaminated sites benefit from a dedicated funding stream for toxic-waste cleanup instead of relying on general taxpayer revenues, and taxpayers generally benefit because polluters rather than the public treasury bear more of the cleanup cost [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund Financing rate on crude oil, raising it from the expired 9.7 cents a barrel to 16.3 cents, adjusted for inflation, through the end of 2023 [S2][S3].
Imposes a new 0.12% corporate environmental income tax on taxable income above $3.13 million (inflation-adjusted), applying to taxable years through 2024 [S2][S3].
Routes the revenue into the Superfund trust fund, restoring the 'polluter pays' financing that lapsed when the original taxes expired [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies pay the per-barrel excise tax — including on exported crude, since the bill removes the export exemption — and profitable corporations pay the 0.12% surtax on income above the threshold [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; large corporations

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on crude oil are typically passed at least partly to consumers through fuel prices, so some of the cost reaches ordinary drivers rather than staying with shareholders [S2].

The taxes are temporary — the barrel fee expires after 2023 and the corporate tax after 2024 — and the corporate surtax at 0.12% is modest, so the bill restores only part of the Superfund's original financing without a permanent fix [S3].

The excise tax applies per barrel of crude regardless of any company's actual connection to a contaminated site, so some firms pay without being linked to specific pollution, and the removal of the export exemption taxes crude sold abroad [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill restores a user-fee structure for toxic-site cleanup that shifts costs from general taxpayers toward the industries whose products generate hazardous substances, at a modest overall price: the rates are temporary and the corporate surtax is small, and some excise cost would reach consumers at the pump. On balance it re-establishes 'polluter pays' funding without large new burdens on working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act on November 14, 2019, joined by Rep. Bill Pascrell Jr. as its only cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies and profitable corporations avoided the new excise tax and surtax, while taxpayers continued to shoulder toxic-waste cleanup costs through general revenues.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate Superfund financing taxes

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Richard Neal)
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair, House Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 14, 2019 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were New Jersey Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split [S1][S4].

industries.note: The bill reinstates a 16.3-cent-per-barrel fee on crude oil (inflation-adjusted) and removes the export exemption, so refiners and producers pay on every barrel including exported crude. Part of the cost would likely reach consumers at the pump.

A new 0.12% surtax applies to taxable income above $3.13 million, hitting large corporations with an additional tax on top of regular income tax; it excludes regulated investment companies and real estate investment trusts.

industries.industry: Environmental remediation and hazardous-waste cleanup contractors
industries.note: Replenishing the Superfund trust fund supports federal cleanup contracts at contaminated sites, work done by remediation firms.
